scope: Runner startup: how long a pipeline run takes to begin, split into node launch, image pull and DuckDB extension load.
timing_scope: Per arm. x1/x2 time the probe process itself (container start to DuckLake attached and queried) at millisecond resolution from the process clock. n1/n2 time the Kubernetes lifecycle (NodeClaim created through container started) at the one-second resolution Kubernetes records, except the image pull, which comes from the kubelet Pulled event message and is sub-second.
isolation: One probe at a time on an otherwise idle dev cluster. n1/n2 run on a dedicated measurement NodePool that is deleted afterwards; x1/x2 run on the always-on app pool alongside the namespace web-api Deployment only.
limitations: The node arms run on a c6id.xlarge probe pool, not runner-sm's c6id.2xlarge. The applied EC2 Standard vCPU quotas are 8 for spot and 8 for on-demand and the always-on app and system nodes hold 2 each, so an 8-vCPU node cannot place at all. Launch, boot and kubelet-join transfer unchanged; the image pull may be marginally optimistic, because Auto Mode's instance-store pull path scales with the number of NVMe devices.

Kubernetes records node-lifecycle conditions at one-second resolution, so the NodeClaim phases are whole seconds. The image pull comes from the kubelet's own Pulled event message and the probe timings from the process clock, both sub-second.

The probe is `er doctor` against a freshly created local DuckLake. It exercises session open, extension load, ATTACH, the lake-schema reconcile and a per-relation count — the whole startup path — but no scoring. This is a startup measurement and says nothing about pipeline throughput.

x2 depends on the egress NetworkPolicy actually being programmed, and the AWS VPC CNI programs it asynchronously after the pod is already running: measured on this cluster, a labelled pod connected at t=0 and was blocked at t=10s. The probe therefore proves its own egress is shut before measuring and exits 2 otherwise, so a mis-programmed policy voids the arm instead of passing it. Every x2 trial here recorded egress_blocked=1.

x1 and x2 run on the always-on app node, whose network path is warm; the extension fetch measured there (~0.85 s) is smaller than on a freshly booted node (n1), so the app-pool figure is a floor for the fetch rather than a typical runner cost.
Karpenter placed the observed probe nodes as on-demand rather than spot, in a single AZ (us-east-2a), on an otherwise idle dev cluster. Spot placement, other AZs and a busy cluster are unmeasured.

A negative fetch delta on the after arm (one trial recorded -27 ms) is noise straddling zero, which is what no-fetch looks like once the first and second sessions become indistinguishable. It is kept rather than clamped.

image_size_comparison.note: Compressed manifest size from ECR. The before figure is the last main-built er-api carrying three binaries and no baked extensions; the after figure is the image measured here. This is the one comparison that needs two images, and it is registry metadata rather than a probe.
image_size_comparison.interpretation: The image GREW. Dropping two of three binaries saved about 17.5 MB compressed — so statically linking DuckDB three times was worth roughly 8.75 MB per binary, far less than the uncompressed 65.6 MB each suggests — while baking five extensions cost about 33 MB. A deliberate trade: a fraction of a second of extra pull, once per node, against the per-process extension fetch and the external dependency.

selection: Both arms run the SAME image; the only variable is whether ER_DUCKDB_EXTENSION_DIR points at the baked directory. Comparing two images would have varied every byte, and the nearest comparable main-built image predated the per-run lake-schema reconcile, so its probe exercised less of the session path and would have understated the cost being established.
promotion_note: The extension bake and the single-binary image are merged, not gated on this record: x1 shows the fetch term going to zero and x2 shows the external dependency removed under a policy verified in force. consolidateAfter 10m is applied to the committed NodePools but reaches a cluster only via `make nodepools`, which nothing runs automatically. The cold-node split is reported for §18.16 and closes D-PULL at rung zero; it licenses no change by itself.

deployment_verification.result: The image boots in the real chart. Both containers run the measured tag; er-server logged "listening on 0.0.0.0:8000" and "dispatcher up"; the in-process dispatcher claimed and classified jobs; and `er --help` inside the running pod prints the pipeline CLI help, which is the multicall symlink working in a deployed pod rather than a test harness.
deployment_verification.side_effect: This also repaired the namespace, which had been down for about three hours: it was pinned to er-api:e3cf6537… (a tag CI never managed to push, because the image build was broken) and to an er-web digest that ECR lifecycle had since garbage-collected. Both now point at a tag that exists.
deployment_verification.known_failure_not_caused_here: The post-upgrade er-tenant-migrate hook fails and leaves the Helm release marked failed, while the Deployment itself is healthy. Cause is pre-existing data: the active org `smoke1` has no ER_LAKE_CATALOG in its env, so its lake_migrate job fails [precondition] and migrate-tenants correctly exits non-zero. Not fixed here — it is someone else dev tenant row, not a code defect.
